verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,
to Timothy, my true child in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
Just as I urged you when I was leaving for Macedonia, stay on in Ephesus, so that you may instruct certain people not to teach anything different

note.traditional: As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus … so do

verse.note: The Greek sentence opens “Just as I urged you to stay on in Ephesus…” and is never grammatically completed. Like most modern translations, this one turns the earlier request into a present instruction; older versions instead supplied “so do” at the end of verse 4. The sense is the same either way.

verse.text: nor to occupy themselves with myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than God’s plan, which works by faith.

note.traditional: godly edifying (KJV); the stewardship from God

verse.note: The word means the management of a household and, by extension, an administration or arrangement. Here it may be God’s own ordering of salvation (“plan”) or the responsibility God entrusts to those who serve him (“stewardship”); both readings have wide support. The KJV’s “godly edifying” follows a different Greek word found in a few manuscripts.

verse.text: But the goal of this instruction is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and a sincere faith.
Some have strayed from these and turned aside into empty talk,
wanting to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they are saying nor the things about which they are so insistent.
Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,

understanding this: law is not laid down for a righteous person but for the lawless and rebellious, the ungodly and sinners, the unholy and profane, those who kill their fathers or mothers, murderers,
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice” all translate the same root. Here the word describes a person who already does what is right, and so is not the target of a code of prohibitions.

verse.text: the sexually immoral, men who lie with males, slave traders, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound teaching,

note.traditional: sodomites; homosexuals; men who practice homosexuality

verse.note: The word is a transparent compound of “male” and “bed” (a common euphemism for intercourse) and is not attested before Paul; most scholars think it was formed from the wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 in the Greek Old Testament. It refers to males who have sex with males, and the rendering keeps to that description of an act instead of using “homosexual,” a modern category of orientation. Whether it covers all male same-sex intercourse or particular forms of it is disputed.

verse.text: in accordance with the good news of the glory of the blessed God, with which I was entrusted.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

verse.text: I am thankful to the one who gave me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to service,
verse.note: Most translations have “ministry” here. The Greek was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and did not denote a religious office; “ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession. Some scholars stress the idea of a commissioned agent over that of humble service, and “service” is compatible with either.

verse.text: though I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a man of arrogant violence. But I was shown mercy, because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief,
and the grace of our Lord overflowed beyond measure, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
The saying is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners—and I am the foremost of them.

note.traditional: This is a faithful saying (KJV); the saying is trustworthy

verse.note: The adjective is the same one rendered “faithful” in verse 12, and this translation normally renders it “faithful” or “believing.” Applied to a saying it means one that can be relied on, and since modern English does not call a statement “faithful,” “trustworthy” is used. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus and appears to mark established Christian sayings.

verse.text: But for this very reason I was shown mercy: so that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display all his patience, as a pattern for those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age,” the same word that appears twice in the next verse. In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase speaks of a kind of life as well as its unending length. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

verse.text: Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verse.note: Many versions paraphrase as “the King eternal”; the Greek says “King of the ages,” meaning the one who rules over every era of history, and some versions render it so. The closing “forever and ever” is literally “to the ages of the ages,” an ordinary idiom for endless time that echoes the title.

verse.text: This instruction I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in keeping with the prophecies made earlier about you, so that by them you may wage the good warfare,

note.term: the prophecies made earlier about you
note.traditional: the prophecies which went before on thee

verse.note: The Greek participle can mean “going before” in time or “leading the way.” The rendering takes it of prophetic words spoken about Timothy on an earlier occasion, perhaps at his commissioning (compare 4:14). The alternative is “the prophecies that led the way to you,” that is, that first pointed Paul to Timothy.

verse.text: holding on to faith and a good conscience. By thrusting conscience aside, some have suffered shipwreck in regard to the faith;
among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan so that they may be taught by discipline not to blaspheme.
verse.note: The same expression occurs in 1 Corinthians 5:5, where it accompanies the removal of a man from the congregation. Most interpreters understand it here as exclusion from the community, the world outside being seen as the sphere of Satan’s power. The stated purpose is corrective: that the two men learn not to blaspheme. Exactly what the procedure involved is not known.

verse.text: First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,
for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.
This is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, himself a human being, Christ Jesus,
verse.note: The Greek word here is the general term for a human being, not the word for a male, and it repeats the word just used for “human beings.” The point is that the mediator shares the nature of those he represents. The traditional “the man Christ Jesus” is not wrong, but it hides the echo and can be heard as a statement about maleness.

verse.text: who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony given at the proper time.

note.term: the testimony given at the proper time
note.traditional: to be testified in due time

verse.note: The Greek is very compressed, literally “the testimony in its own times,” and “given” is supplied. Most interpreters take it to mean that Christ’s self-giving is itself the witness to God’s saving purpose, borne at the time God appointed. It can also be read as pointing forward to the message that the writer was appointed to proclaim (verse 7).

verse.text: For this I was appointed a herald and an apostle—I am telling the truth; I am not lying—a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”; in Jewish usage the plural names the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the same word “nations” where peoples as such are in view and “Gentiles” where, as here, the contrast with Israel is the point.

verse.text: So I want the men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument.
verse.note: Standing with hands raised and palms open was the ordinary posture of prayer among both Jews and Greeks. The emphasis falls not on the gesture, which is assumed, but on the hands being “holy” and the prayer being free of anger.

The word can mean inner reasoning or doubt, or an outward dispute. Paired with “anger” and addressed to men praying together, it is usually taken as disputing, and that reading is followed here. Older versions have “doubting,” which remains possible.

verse.text: Likewise, I want women to adorn themselves in respectable attire, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or expensive clothing,

note.term: braided hair and gold or pearls
note.traditional: braided hair, or gold, or pearls

verse.note: Elaborate hairstyles interwoven with gold and jewels were a conspicuous display of wealth among well-to-do women of the period, and Greek and Roman moralists made similar criticisms. The concern is ostentation in the assembly, not braiding as such.

verse.text: but, as is fitting for women who profess reverence for God, with good works.
A woman is to learn in quietness, in all submission.
verse.note: Older versions have “silence.” The word more often describes a calm, settled, undisruptive manner than the absence of speech; its adjective is used in verse 2 for the “quiet” life believers hope to lead. Many modern translations accordingly have “quietly” or “quietness,” though some scholars still argue for “silence” here.

verse.text: I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to be in quietness.

note.traditional: usurp authority over; have authority over

verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament and is rare in Greek of the period, so its exact force is disputed. Some scholars take it neutrally (“have” or “exercise authority”), others negatively (“domineer over”) or as “assume authority” on one’s own initiative. The evidence does not settle the question; the rendering here follows the neutral reading found in most modern translations.

The Greek words for “woman” and “man” are also the ordinary words for “wife” and “husband,” and the appeal to Adam and Eve that follows concerns a married pair. Most translations take verses 8–15 to be about men and women in the gathered community; a minority of scholars read verses 11–15 as concerning wives and husbands.

verse.text: For Adam was formed first, then Eve;
and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression.
But she will be saved through childbearing, if they remain in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verse.note: This is one of the most debated phrases in the letter. The Greek has the article (“the childbearing”), and the main proposals are: saved through the role of bearing and raising children; brought safely through childbirth; or saved through the birth of the child, meaning the Messiah born of a woman. The rendering here leaves the phrase as open as the Greek does.

The Greek shifts without explanation from the singular “she will be saved” to the plural “they remain.” “She” most naturally picks up “the woman” of verse 14, Eve as representing women, and “they” is usually taken as women generally. Others suggest it means the woman and her husband, or her children.

verse.text: The saying is trustworthy: if anyone aspires to the role of overseer, he desires a good work.
verse.note: This adjective is normally rendered “faithful” or “believing” in this translation, but modern English does not call a statement “faithful”; “trustworthy” expresses the same idea of reliability. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus. Most interpreters take it here as introducing the saying about overseers, though some attach it to the end of the previous chapter.

verse.text: So the overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, clear-headed, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verse.note: In ordinary Greek the word meant a supervisor or guardian and was used of officials of various kinds. “Bishop” descends from it but now suggests a single cleric governing a diocese, an arrangement that developed later; most modern translations also use “overseer”. The related noun in verse 1 is rendered “the role of overseer”.

The Greek is literally “a man of one woman”. It may mean faithful to his wife, married only once (excluding remarriage after a death or divorce), or not having more than one wife at a time. The traditional wording is kept because it leaves the question open; many recent interpreters favor marital faithfulness, but the matter is disputed. The same phrase is used of deacons in verse 12.

verse.text: not a drunkard, not violent, but gentle, peaceable, not a lover of money,
managing his own household well, keeping his children in submission with all dignity.
(If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s assembly?)
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Scriptures, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: He must not be a new convert, so that he does not become conceited and fall into the judgment passed on the devil.

note.term: the judgment passed on the devil

verse.note: The Greek is simply “the judgment of the devil”. Most interpreters understand it as the judgment the devil himself incurred, with pride as the link, and the text follows that reading. It could also mean a judgment the devil brings about, as accuser, which would parallel “the devil’s snare” in the next verse.

verse.text: He must also be well spoken of by those outside, so that he does not fall into disgrace and the devil’s snare.
Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain,
holding the revealed secret of the faith with a clean conscience.

note.term: the revealed secret of the faith

verse.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. Most English versions keep “mystery” as a technical term, but that word now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas the point here is that the thing has been made known. “Revealed” is added because a bare “secret of the faith” would be heard as “the key to faith”; the same wording is used in verse 16.

verse.text: And these too must first be tested; then let them serve as deacons, if they prove blameless.
Women likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, clear-headed, faithful in everything.
verse.note: The Greek word means both “woman” and “wife”, and there is no “their” in the text. The verse may refer to women who serve as deacons or to the wives of deacons; the parallel “likewise” and the list of qualifications favor the first, while the position of the verse in the middle of the instructions for deacons is taken by some to favor the second. The rendering leaves the question open.

verse.text: Deacons must each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.
For those who have served well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verse.note: The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind and by this period also the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. “Boldness” can suggest nerve or audacity, which is not the point here; many modern versions likewise have “confidence” or “assurance”. The difference is one of English nuance, not a dispute about meaning.

verse.text: I am writing these things to you, though I hope to come to you soon,
so that, if I am delayed, you may know how one must behave in God’s household, which is the assembly of the living God, a pillar and support of the truth.
verse.note: The same Greek word is used in verses 4, 5 and 12 for the household an overseer or deacon must manage, and the argument depends on that link: the assembly is God’s family and establishment, not a building. “House of God” is the traditional rendering and could also evoke the temple, an image the following “pillar” may continue. Several modern versions also have “household”.

verse.text: And undeniably great is the revealed secret of godliness: He appeared in flesh, was vindicated in spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the Gentiles, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.

note.traditional: God was manifest in the flesh

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “who” (rendered here “He”), and this is the reading of nearly all modern editions. Later manuscripts read “God”, which in abbreviated Greek script differs from “who” by only two small strokes; this is the source of the traditional rendering. The six short, balanced lines that follow are widely thought to be an early hymn or confession about Christ that the letter quotes.

The verb belongs to the word family elsewhere rendered “righteousness” and “justify”; here the sense is that he was shown to be in the right, most likely by the resurrection, so “vindicated” is used, as in many modern versions. “In spirit” is taken as the counterpart of “in flesh”, the spiritual realm set against the human one. It may also be read “by the Spirit”, meaning God’s Spirit, and versions are divided.

The same Greek plural means both “nations” and “Gentiles”, the non-Jewish peoples. “Among the nations” is equally possible here and is preferred by many versions, since the line is paired with “angels” and followed by “the world”. “Gentiles” is kept because proclamation to the non-Jewish peoples is a stated concern of this letter.

verse.text: Now the Spirit says explicitly that in later times some will fall away from the faith, devoting themselves to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons
through the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience has been seared,
verse.note: The verb means to burn with a hot iron. It can picture a conscience cauterized into numbness, as rendered here, or a conscience “branded,” as slaves and criminals were, with a mark of ownership (here, by the demonic powers of verse 1). Both readings have scholarly support, and the Greek does not decide between them.

verse.text: who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and have come to know the truth.
For everything God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving,
for it is made holy through the word of God and prayer.
verse.note: Most translations have “sanctified” or “consecrated.” The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “made holy” keeps that link audible. The meaning is not in dispute; the point is that food received with thanks belongs within the sphere of what is God’s, against those who declare it off limits.

note.term: the word of God and prayer
note.traditional: the word of God and prayer

verse.note: What “the word of God” refers to is debated. It may be God’s declaration in Genesis that what he made is good, scriptural phrases used in thanksgiving at meals, or the gospel message. The second noun is a word for petition or prayer addressed to God, here evidently the thanksgiving said over food.

verse.text: If you put these things before the brothers and sisters, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and of the good teaching that you have followed.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, here the whole community of believers. “Brothers” alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are meant. Many recent translations make the same choice.

verse.text: But have nothing to do with profane old wives’ tales. Train yourself instead for godliness;
verse.note: Literally “myths of the kind old women tell.” This was a stock expression of contempt in ancient philosophical debate for stories considered unworthy of serious attention. It dismisses the opponents’ teaching and is not a comment on older women as such.

verse.text: for physical training is beneficial to a small extent, but godliness is beneficial in every way, since it holds a promise of life, both the present life and the life to come.
verse.note: The Greek phrase is literally “for a little” and can mean either “to a limited degree” or “for a short time.” The contrast with “in every way” favors the first, but the reference to the present life and the life to come gives the second some support.

verse.text: The saying is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance,
verse.note: This adjective is normally rendered “faithful” or “believing” in this translation. Applied to a saying it means reliable or worthy of trust, and “a faithful saying” would now suggest a statement that accurately reproduces some original, so “trustworthy” is used for this formula.

This formula occurs five times in the letters to Timothy and Titus. Here it is unclear whether it points back to the statement about godliness in verse 8 or forward to verse 10. Most interpreters take it with verse 8, but the question is open.

verse.text: for this is why we labor and are insulted: because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between “we are insulted” (the reading of the Greek text translated here, and of the King James tradition) and “we struggle,” which differs by a few letters and is followed by many modern translations. Both readings are ancient and editors disagree about which is original.

The usual meaning of the word is “especially,” which makes God the Savior of all people in some sense and of believers in a fuller one. Some scholars argue that it can mean “that is to say,” which would limit the statement to believers. That sense is disputed and is not adopted here.

verse.text: Command these things and teach them.
Let no one look down on you for being young, but become an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading, to exhortation, to teaching.
verse.note: The noun refers to reading aloud to a gathering, not private study. In synagogue and church the Scriptures were read out to the assembled community, most of whom did not own or could not read books, and the reading was followed by exhortation and teaching, the two activities named next.

verse.text: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of hands by the council of elders.
Practice these things; be immersed in them, so that your progress may be plain to everyone.
Keep watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in these things, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.
Do not speak harshly to an older man, but appeal to him as a father, to younger men as brothers,
verse.note: The Greek word is the same one translated “elders” in verses 17 and 19, where it names a leadership role. Here it is set alongside younger men, older women and younger women, so nearly all interpreters take it as a matter of age. Older versions have “an elder.”

verse.text: to older women as mothers, to younger women as sisters, in all purity.
Honor widows who are really widows.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both showing respect and providing material support, as the related noun does in verse 17. The discussion that follows, about who should provide for widows and who should be enrolled, shows that practical support is in view as well as esteem.

verse.text: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to show piety toward their own household and to repay their parents and grandparents, for this is acceptable before God.
verse.note: The Greek does not state who “they” are. Most interpreters take the subject to be the children and grandchildren, who owe care to the widow who raised them. A minority take it to be the widows, who should first attend to their own households.

verse.text: The one who is really a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in petitions and prayers night and day;
but the one who lives for pleasure is dead while she lives.
Command these things as well, so that they may be above reproach.
But if anyone does not provide for their own people, and especially for members of their household, that person has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
A widow should be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one husband,
verse.note: Literally “a woman of one man,” mirroring the requirement for overseers in 3:2. It may mean a woman who was married only once, or one who was faithful to her husband. Because verse 14 urges younger widows to remarry, many scholars favor the second reading, but the question is disputed.

verse.text: well attested for good works: if she has brought up children, if she has shown hospitality to strangers, if she has washed the feet of the holy ones, if she has helped those in distress, if she has devoted herself to every good work.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God's people.”

verse.text: But refuse younger widows; for when their desires draw them away from Christ, they want to marry,

note.term: their desires draw them away from Christ
note.traditional: they have begun to wax wanton against Christ

verse.note: The verb occurs only here in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere. A related word describes unrestrained, luxurious living, and the compound here suggests strong impulses, probably sexual, that run against Christ. Its exact nuance is uncertain.

verse.text: and so incur judgment, because they have set aside their first pledge.
verse.note: This is the word normally rendered “faith,” but here it is the object of a verb meaning to annul or break, a combination found in Greek writers for going back on one's word. Most modern translations therefore have “pledge,” understood as a commitment to remain unmarried in Christ's service made when a widow was enrolled. The older rendering “their first faith” takes it as abandoning their original Christian faith, and remains possible.

verse.text: At the same time they also learn to be idle, going around from house to house—and not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
So I want younger women to marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no opening for abuse.
For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.
If any believing woman has widows in her care, let her help them, and let the assembly not be burdened, so that it may help those who are really widows.

note.traditional: any man or woman that believeth

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “believing man or woman.” The earliest witnesses have only the feminine, which is the reading translated here. It probably envisages a woman of some means with widows in her household or among her dependents.

The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: The elders who lead well should be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in speaking and teaching.
verse.note: The Greek noun means both respect and payment, and the two quotations in verse 18 about feeding the ox and paying the worker show that material support is included. Whether “double” means twice what the enrolled widows received, respect plus pay, or simply generous provision is uncertain.

verse.text: For the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

note.term: “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

verse.note: The first quotation is from Deuteronomy 25:4. The second matches a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke 10:7. It is debated whether “the Scripture says” is meant to cover both, or only the first, with the second added as a familiar saying.

verse.text: Do not accept an accusation against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.
Those who are sinning, rebuke before everyone, so that the rest also may be afraid.
I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels to keep these things without prejudging, doing nothing out of favoritism.
Do not be quick to lay hands on anyone, and do not share in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verse.note: Laying on of hands was the gesture by which a person was appointed to a role in the community, as in 4:14. Most interpreters take this as a warning against appointing elders hastily. A minority see it as the readmission of those who had sinned.

verse.text: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.
verse.note: The Greek verb describes someone who drinks water and abstains from wine as a practice. The point is that Timothy should stop abstaining, not stop drinking water. Wine was widely regarded as beneficial for digestion in the ancient world.

verse.text: The sins of some people are plain to see, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others follow after them.
In the same way good works too are plain to see, and those that are not cannot stay hidden.
All who are under the yoke as slaves must regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed.

Those who have believing masters must not look down on them because they are brothers; instead they must serve them all the more, because those who benefit from their good service are believers and beloved. Teach these things and urge them.

note.term: those who benefit from their good service

verse.note: The Greek can be read two ways. On the reading adopted here, which most modern translations share, the masters are the ones who receive the benefit of the slaves’ service. The verb can also mean “devote oneself to”, which would give “those who devote themselves to doing good are believers and beloved”. The word for “good service” normally described the benefaction of a superior, so applying it to a slave’s work is striking.

verse.text: If anyone teaches something different and does not agree with the sound words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the teaching that accords with godliness,
that person is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing, but is sick with a craving for controversies and battles over words. From these come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions,

note.traditional: doting about; has an unhealthy craving

verse.note: The verb means to be ill, and it is set against the “sound” (literally “healthy”) words of verse 3. The letter pictures correct teaching as health and the opponents’ obsession with disputes as a disease. Scholars differ on how strongly the medical image was felt, but the pairing here suggests it is deliberate.

verse.text: and constant friction among people who are corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain.
And godliness with contentment is indeed a great means of gain;
verse.note: The Greek word was a prized term in popular philosophy, especially among Stoics and Cynics, for self-sufficiency: needing nothing beyond what one has. The related verb appears in verse 8 (“we will be content”). The sentence also plays on verse 5: the opponents think godliness is a “means of gain”, and the writer agrees, in a sense they did not intend.

verse.text: for we brought nothing into the world, and neither can we carry anything out of it;

note.term: and neither can we carry anything out of it
note.traditional: and it is certain we can carry nothing out

verse.note: The connecting word in the earliest manuscripts normally means “because” or “that”, which gives an awkward logic (“we brought nothing in because we can take nothing out”). Later manuscripts smooth this by adding “it is clear that” or “it is true that”, which lies behind the King James rendering. Most modern translations, as here, treat the connection as a loose “and” or “so”.

verse.text: but having food and clothing, we will be content with these.
But those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare and many senseless and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction;
for the love of money is a root of all evils. Some, reaching for it, have been led astray from the faith and have pierced themselves with many pains.

note.traditional: the root of all evil; a root of all kinds of evil

verse.note: The Greek has no article with “root”, and it can be read as “a root” or, in a proverbial saying like this, “the root”. The following phrase is literally “of all the evils”; many modern versions soften it to “all kinds of evil”, but the Greek does not say “kinds”. The saying resembles proverbs about greed current in the period and is best heard as a sweeping maxim, not a precise claim about the cause of every wrong.

verse.text: But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. Here, in a list of qualities to pursue, the word means upright conduct, doing what is right. “Righteousness” is the standard rendering; some translators prefer “justice”.

verse.text: Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verse.note: The verb and its noun come from the world of athletic contests, where competitors struggled for a prize, and were widely used for any strenuous effort. The picture is of a contest in the arena as much as of warfare; “compete in the good contest” would also be a fair rendering.

The adjective is formed from the word for “age”. In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of its kind as well as its unending length. Verse 19 calls the same thing “the life that is truly life”, and verse 17 contrasts it with “the present age”.

verse.text: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who testified to the good confession before Pontius Pilate,
verse.note: The preposition can mean “in the presence of”, pointing to Jesus’ testimony at his trial, or “in the time of”, as in the creeds’ “under Pontius Pilate”, which would point to his whole witness culminating in his death. Most translations take it as “before”, and that reading is followed here.

verse.text: to keep the commandment unstained and beyond reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
which the blessed and only Sovereign will display at the right time—the King of kings and Lord of lords,
who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human being has seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal power. Amen.
Charge those who are rich in the present age not to be arrogant or to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment;
verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, not the word for “world” used in verse 7. New Testament writers share the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come, and that contrast is the point here: wealth belongs to this age, while verse 19 looks to “the future”. Several modern versions also render “present age”.

verse.text: charge them to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,
storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, turning away from the profane empty talk and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge;

note.traditional: science falsely so called; what is falsely called knowledge

verse.note: The opponents evidently claimed a special “knowledge” (Greek gnosis), and the word for “contradictions” may refer to their debating propositions or counter-arguments. Whether this is connected with the Gnostic movements known from the second century is disputed; the letter gives too little detail to be sure. The King James “science” meant “knowledge” in older English.

verse.text: by professing it, some have missed the mark concerning the faith. Grace be with you.
verse.note: In the earliest manuscripts “you” is plural, which suggests the letter, though addressed to Timothy, was expected to be heard by the congregation. Many later manuscripts have the singular “you” and add “Amen”, readings reflected in the King James Version.
